chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from his father, from Abu al-Mi'za, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār, from al-ʿAbd al-Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who is obligated to travel to the House of God (for Hajj) and does not buy clothes for his family using deferred payment (nasi'ah) for a year. He said, 'That harms them and is difficult for them.' I said, 'Yes, it is difficult for them.' He said, 'Let him buy for them, and there is no penalty upon him.'

key_terms.بَيْتِ اللَّهِ: The House of God (referring to the Kaaba in Mecca)
key_terms.بِالنَّسِيئَةِ: With deferred payment / credit (a form of sale where payment is delayed)
key_terms.وَلَا شَيْءَ عَلَيْهِ: And there is nothing (penalty/sin) upon him

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a man buying clothes for his family on credit while he is away performing Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the obligation of Hajj does not exempt a man from providing for his family's basic needs, specifically clothing. He rules that if delaying purchases for a year causes hardship (*yashquq*), the man may use credit (*al-nasi'ah*) without sin, prioritizing familial welfare (*nafaqah*) over the immediate timing of the pilgrimage. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that religious duties are balanced with the practical removal of hardship (*raf' al-haraj*) for dependents.
